summaries.example: Imagine two people with stomach pain. One has a temporary ache after eating too much. The other has an inflamed body system that is not working normally. A naturalist may say the second case is a disease because a body system is malfunctioning and causing harm. A constructivist may ask why society chooses to treat some harmful conditions as medical problems and others as something else.
summaries.summary: This entry explores what people mean by “disease” and “health.” One group of philosophers, called naturalists, says disease includes a real malfunction in the body or mind. Another group, called constructivists, says that human values and social practices help decide which conditions receive medical labels. Many views combine both ideas: a biological condition may be important, but people must also judge whether it causes a kind of harm that medicine should address. The entry also explains that deciding what counts as normal is difficult because living things vary. Health is debated too. It might mean that the body works well, that a person can pursue important goals, or that the person feels able to take part in life. These ideas do not always match. A person may have a disease without knowing it, or may feel unhappy for reasons that are not diseases.
key_ideas: Philosophers ask whether disease is mainly a biological problem, a judgment about harm, or both.
Naturalists give an important role to bodily functions and scientific evidence.
Constructivists emphasize human values, social rules, and the history of medical labels.
A condition can be unusual without being a disease, and a common condition can still be harmful.
Health may mean more than simply having no disease; it may also involve living well or being able to pursue important goals.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ideas about health and disease affect doctors, patients, schools, insurance, and public rules. They can help people receive care, but medical labels can also be used unfairly when society mistakes difference or disapproval for illness. Thinking carefully about these ideas encourages us to ask what evidence supports a diagnosis, what kind of harm is involved, and whose values are shaping the decision.

important_terms.definition: The idea that diseases involve real problems in how body or mind systems work. Science is important for finding those problems.
The idea that people and societies help shape what counts as a disease by using ideas about harm, normality, and medical treatment.
A job or contribution that a body part or system normally makes, such as the heart pumping blood.
A condition in which a body or mind system does not work in the way it normally should.
A way of judging whether something is healthy or unhealthy compared with a usual pattern or an ideal model.

questions_to_think_about: Is every unusual body feature a disease?
How could doctors tell the difference between illness and a condition that society merely dislikes?
Can a body system work normally even when a person feels unwell?
Should health mean only that the body works properly?

summaries.example: Consider high blood pressure. It may be treated as a disease even when a person has no obvious symptoms or a single damaged organ. A naturalist might explain the diagnosis through abnormal regulation or function within the body, together with the risks it creates. A constructivist may focus on how medical communities select a cutoff, decide which risks matter, and organize treatment around that classification. The case shows why biological facts, statistical standards, and value judgments can all enter debates about disease.
summaries.summary: The entry examines competing accounts of health and disease in philosophy of medicine. Naturalism treats disease as grounded in abnormal biological or psychological functioning. Some naturalists add a second condition: the malfunction must make a person worse off or create a reason for medical concern. Constructivism gives priority to evaluative and social factors, arguing that communities help determine which biological differences are labeled pathological and which are treated as ordinary variation, moral deviation, or another kind of problem. Constructivism is supported by historical cases in which social prejudice influenced diagnosis, but it must explain why only some forms of disadvantage become specifically medical concerns. Naturalism faces its own difficulties. It must identify relevant functions, distinguish pathology from widespread variation, select appropriate reference classes, and decide whether normality is statistical or an idealized scientific standard. The entry also discusses conservative and revisionist versions of both approaches. Finally, it considers health as biological efficiency, a positive condition beyond the absence of disease, a lived relation to one’s body and environment, or a capacity to pursue important goals. None of these proposals settles every case.
key_ideas: The central dispute concerns whether biological malfunction or evaluative judgment has conceptual priority in defining disease.
Naturalist theories must explain what counts as a genuine function, how reference classes are chosen, and how normality differs from mere statistical frequency.
Constructivist theories explain the influence of social values and medical practices but face the challenge of distinguishing medical disapproval from other kinds of disapproval.
Disease, illness, and health can be separated: bodily malfunction, the harmful effect on a person, and broader well-being need not be identical.
There is disagreement about whether biological functions are evolutionary roles, causal contributions within systems, or idealized standards used by biomedical science.
Health may involve biological efficiency, lived experience, adaptation, or the ability to pursue important goals, but defining it as overall well-being may make the concept too broad.
summaries.why_it_matters: Classifications of disease guide diagnosis, treatment, research, insurance, and public policy. They also affect how people understand themselves. A category can identify a real biological problem, but it can also reflect social assumptions or be applied beyond its evidence. The philosophical debate therefore matters for deciding how medicine should use ordinary concepts, when scientific inquiry should revise them, and how to avoid confusing illness with difference, disadvantage, or social disapproval.

important_terms.definition: A family of views holding that disease depends fundamentally on objectively discoverable biological or psychological malfunction, although some versions also include an evaluative judgment about harm.
A family of views holding that disease categories are shaped, or even constituted, by human values, social practices, and judgments about which conditions count as medical problems.
The position that a concept should be changed when inquiry shows that ordinary usage or common intuitions interfere with scientific or practical goals.
The position that ordinary language and common judgments should place limits on a philosophical or scientific account of health and disease.
An account that treats disease as involving both a causal biological basis and an evaluative judgment that the resulting condition is harmful or calls for action.
A model of biological function based on what a structure contributes to the operation of a larger system, rather than on its evolutionary history.
A model of function based on effects that helped a trait spread through natural selection; dysfunction is then understood as failure of that selected role.

questions_to_think_about: Can a disease concept be objective if deciding its boundaries requires a conventional cutoff?
Does a history of mistaken diagnoses show that disease is socially constructed, or only that a naturalistic concept was misapplied?
What reference class should determine whether a biological trait is functioning normally?
How should a theory distinguish health from general well-being?
Should scientific accounts of disease revise everyday language when the two conflict?

summaries.example: Suppose a student has trouble concentrating because of a temporary lack of sleep. Another student has a condition involving a psychological system that is not working properly and is causing serious problems in daily life. A naturalist would look for evidence of the system’s malfunction. A constructivist might also ask how schools, families, and medical professionals decided that this kind of problem belongs in the category of illness rather than being treated only as a behavior issue. The example shows that causes and social judgments can both matter.
summaries.summary: The entry asks a basic but difficult question: what makes something a disease rather than simply a difference, a problem, or a kind of suffering? Naturalists say disease involves a real malfunction in bodily or mental systems. Some naturalists add that the malfunction must also harm a person or create a reason for treatment. Constructivists emphasize that communities decide, through values and practices, which conditions count as medical problems. They point out that diagnoses have sometimes reflected social prejudice rather than good science. Critics reply that people usually distinguish illness from other things they dislike, so constructivists need to explain what makes a judgment specifically medical. Naturalists face another challenge: humans show lots of variation, and what is statistically common is not always healthy. A textbook picture of an ideal organ may be more useful than a simple average. The entry also distinguishes conservative theories, which protect ordinary meanings, from revisionist theories, which allow science or social criticism to change them. For health, possible accounts focus on proper biological functioning, a person’s experience, adaptation, or the ability to pursue important goals.
key_ideas: The naturalist and constructivist approaches disagree about which part of the explanation comes first: biological malfunction or judgments about harm.
Both approaches recognize that medical thinking involves more than simply noticing that someone is different.
Naturalism has to explain how science can identify normal function when people vary widely.
Constructivism has to explain why some disliked or harmful conditions become medical problems while others do not.
Health may be more than the absence of disease; it may include well-being, flexibility, lived experience, or the ability to reach important goals.
summaries.why_it_matters: The meaning of health and disease affects who receives care and how people are treated. A good definition can help doctors identify problems, but a poor definition can turn harmless differences into medical defects or hide the role of social conditions in causing harm. Understanding the debate helps us examine evidence, question labels carefully, and separate biological illness from unfair treatment or ordinary human variation.

important_terms.definition: The view that disease depends on facts about how human bodies or minds function, especially whether important systems are working correctly.
The view that people’s values and social practices help create or shape the categories used for health and disease.
A bodily or mental process failing to carry out an important job it normally performs.
The job a body part, process, or system performs within a living organism.
A judgment about what is usual, proper, or expected in a group or situation.
A view that disease includes both a biological cause and a judgment that the resulting condition is harmful or needs attention.
A standard group used for comparison when deciding whether a trait or performance is typical.

questions_to_think_about: If a condition is common, must it be healthy?
If a condition is rare, must it be a disease?
Can a society’s unfair values influence medical diagnoses?
What makes a problem medical instead of social, legal, or moral?
Is someone healthy if their body works normally but they cannot pursue important goals?
